title: Scotch Eggs
subtitle: Soft-boiled eggs wrapped in sausage meat and fried
excerpt: A soft-boiled egg at the centre of a seasoned pork sausage meat shell, coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried until golden. Best eaten still warm, with the yolk just runny. A British pub classic.

recipe.sourceNotes: The Scotch egg was invented in 1738 by the London department store Fortnum and Mason, intended as a portable snack for travellers. Despite the name, the dish has no Scottish origin. The commercial version uses hard-boiled eggs; the refined pub version uses soft-boiled eggs with a runny yolk. The traditional accompaniment is English mustard and pickles. The sausage layer is seasoned with herbs and sometimes Dijon mustard mixed into the meat.

content.text: The key temperatures: eggs in cold water, bring to boil, 6 minutes, cold water immediately. This gives a set white with a soft yolk. Chill the coated eggs in the fridge for 20 minutes before frying to help them hold their shape. Fry at 170 C: too hot and the crumbs burn before the sausage meat is cooked through; too cool and the eggs absorb excess oil.
Place 4 eggs in cold water. Bring to a boil, then cook for 6 minutes. Transfer to cold water. Once cool, peel carefully.

Mix the sausage meat with the Dijon mustard, thyme, salt, and pepper. Divide into 4 equal portions. Flatten each portion in your palm. Place a peeled egg in the centre and wrap the meat around it, sealing any gaps. Refrigerate for 20 minutes.
Beat the 2 remaining eggs. Set up three shallow bowls: flour, beaten egg, and breadcrumbs. Roll each Scotch egg in flour, then beaten egg, then breadcrumbs. Press the crumbs on firmly.
Heat the oil to 170 C in a deep saucepan. Fry the eggs 2 at a time for 6 to 7 minutes until deep golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper. Eat warm with English mustard.
